newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's LVMH cuts stake in Guinness.
newsitem.headline: France's LVMH cuts stake in Guinness.

text.p: French luxury goods group LVMH sold a third of its stake in British drinks company and longtime ally Guinness Plc Friday, further diluting the role of the slow-growing liquor business in its empire.

"LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton has sold 135,081,327 shares of Guinness, equivalent to approximately 7 percent of the shares outstanding, to Goldman Sachs, thereby reducing its stake to approximately 14 percent," LVMH said in a statement.

Investment firm Goldman Sachs was placing the shares on the market at 414 pence, dealers said, putting the total value of the sale at 559 million pounds ($935 million), or 5.05 billion francs ($933 million).
A spokeswoman for LVMH said the sale would pay for part of the group's 12.9 billion franc ($2.39 billion) purchase of a majority stake in U.S. duty free chain DFS, concluded earlier this month.
She said the decision to sell part of the Guinness stake reflected a shift in LVMH's horizon. "It's a little more DFS, a little less Guinness."

Industry analysts said the acquisition of DFS, which has 180 shops along the Pacific Rim, and the reduction of LVMH's stake in Guinness underscore the French group's strategy to focus on its most lucrative businesses.

"Guinness is an outstanding franchise, but the economics of the luxury business are better than those of the spirits business. The consumption of alcohol is not as robust as it once was," said Cedric Magnelia at brokerage CS First Boston.

"LVMH is getting more and more involved in luxury goods, where the potential is much higher. You have the developing markets, particularly southeast Asia, which are growing very fast," said Cecile d'Estais at Paribas Capital Markets.
She said the timing for the sale was right because of the British pound's recent rise against the franc.

LVMH said it would keep the remaining 14 percent stake in Guinness and develop the business ties between the two companies, which have 15 joint ventures, including one that handles the distribution of their brands in the United States.

The two companies forged a commercial partnership in the 1980s and followed it up with cross-shareholdings that left Guinness with a 34 percent stake in Moet Hennessy. But the alliance began to weaken as the gap between the profitability of the drinks and luxury goods industries widened.

Last year LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault put pressure on Guinness publicly to increase shareholder value. "Arnault was clearly disappointed in Guinness's share price performance and in the value of his stake in the company," Magnelia said.

Analyst Marie Laure Favre-Gilly at Natwest Sellier said she expected LVMH to keep the 14 percent stake in the short term, in part to protect Guinness's share price. "But I have my doubts about the long term," she said.
